# Results — Study 435 (Guppy Multiple MA) on real daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Daryl Guppy's twin-ribbon
trend filter (GMMA): a short "trader" ribbon of EMAs (3, 5, 8, 10, 12, 15 days) and a
long "investor" ribbon (30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 60 days). The folk reading: be long when the
short ribbon trades above the long ribbon, and trust the trend most when the ribbons are
**wide apart** (conviction). We turn this into a long/flat timing rule, race its
**excess-of-cash** Sharpe against buy-and-hold, a random-timing control, and the obvious
single-moving-average benchmark, with a HAC *t*, a permutation placebo, and a cost sweep.
Tested on SPY daily total-return closes 1993-01-29 → 2026-06-12 (n = 8,400). Cash leg
credited at a flat 4%/yr proxy (FRED unavailable). One-way cost = 2 bps × NAV; one-day
execution lag. As-of **2026-06-13**.*

## Data stamp

| Ticker | Window | n days | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| SPY | 1993-01-29 → 2026-06-12 | 8,400 | `42b159a9d39a` |

## The arms — race on excess-of-cash returns (long/flat, 2 bps one-way)

A binary in/out rule earns the cash rate when flat, so every Sharpe below is on the
**excess-of-cash** series — an excess-vs-excess race. The GMMA ribbon cross is pinned
against buy-and-hold, a random-timing control (same in-market fraction, random days), and
the obvious simpler benchmarks (a single 50-day SMA / EMA filter).

| Arm | CAGR (excess) | Sharpe (excess) | Vol | Max DD | HAC *t* (mean daily) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **Buy-and-hold** | **+6.47%** | **+0.431** | 18.6% | −64.0% | **+2.89** |
| GMMA ribbon cross | +2.80% | +0.301 | 11.3% | −47.5% | +1.86 |
| GMMA conviction-gated | +1.42% | +0.210 | 8.4% | −38.0% | +1.30 |
| Single 50-day SMA | +1.77% | +0.215 | 11.0% | −54.7% | +1.31 |
| Single 50-day EMA | +3.16% | +0.337 | 11.1% | −42.7% | +2.09 |
| Random timing (null) | +3.36% | +0.288 | 15.8% | −60.7% | +1.81 |

- **The ribbon's own *t* falls short.** Its excess HAC *t* = **+1.86** does not clear the
  desk's **|*t*| ≥ 2** inference bar. Buy-and-hold's own excess return *does* (+2.89).
- **It loses the race to buy-and-hold.** The HAC *t* on the daily return *difference*
  (ribbon − BH) = **−2.10** — i.e. buy-and-hold is *significantly better*, not the GMMA.
- **It barely beats a coin.** vs the random-timing control: *t* = **−0.50** (worse, not
  better). The ribbon's lower drawdown is reduced exposure, not timing skill.
- **It does not beat one line.** A single 50-day EMA (Sharpe +0.337) *out-Sharpes* the
  twelve-line ribbon (+0.301); ribbon vs SMA *t* = +1.26 (not significant). The ornate
  ribbon adds nothing over a single moving average.
- **In-market fraction:** 71.7% of days long; 259 switches over 33 years (~8/yr).

## The conviction test — does ribbon *width* reveal a continuing trend?

Guppy's distinctive claim is that a **wide, parallel** separation signals conviction and
the trend will continue. We gate the long leg on the normalised ribbon spread exceeding its
own trailing 60-day median (the ribbon wider than usual). The result is the opposite of the
claim: gating on width **lowers** every number — Sharpe falls from +0.301 to **+0.210**,
CAGR from +2.80% to +1.42%, and conviction-vs-ribbon *t* = **−1.30**. Wide ribbons do not
mark trades worth holding; the width signal is, if anything, a mild contrarian tell.

## Permutation placebo

We circularly rotate the (lagged) ribbon signal 2,000 times — destroying its alignment with
returns while preserving its in-market fraction and autocorrelation — and ask how often a
rotated signal earns at least the real one's mean excess return.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|--:|
| Real ribbon mean excess (bps/day) | +2.55 |
| Mean of rotated placebos (bps/day) | +3.39 |
| **Permutation p-value** | **0.969** |

The real signal underperforms **97%** of random rotations. The GMMA's timing carries no
information the market's overall drift does not already give a random in/out schedule.

## Cost sensitivity (ribbon cross, excess Sharpe)

The rule is low-turnover, so costs are not what kills it — it is dead even gross:

| One-way cost | Sharpe (excess) |
|---|--:|
| 0 bps (gross) | +0.315 |
| 2 bps | +0.301 |
| 5 bps | +0.280 |
| 10 bps | +0.246 |

Even **gross of all costs**, the ribbon's excess Sharpe (+0.315) trails buy-and-hold
(+0.431). There is no cost level at which the rule wins; the gap is structural, not frictional.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness can detect a real trend edge

A faithful-engine check on a deterministic two-regime tape (`data.synthetic_panel`). With a
**planted** bull/bear edge the ribbon *should* beat buy-and-hold by dodging the deep bears;
on a flat random-walk **null** it should add nothing.

| Tape | Ribbon Sharpe | BH Sharpe | *t* (ribbon − BH) | Permutation p |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Planted edge | +0.264 | −0.149 | **+2.35** | **0.0135** |
| Flat null | +0.306 | +0.323 | −0.85 | 0.267 |

On the planted tape the ribbon beats BH at *t* = +2.35 and the permutation p drops to 0.014
(signal in the right tail); on the null it matches BH and p ≈ 0.27. The engine *can* bank a
real trend edge — so its failure to find one in SPY is evidence, not a broken harness.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** The GMMA ribbon's excess HAC *t* = **+1.86** (below the 2-bar), it is
  *significantly worse* than buy-and-hold (race *t* = −2.10), no better than a random
  in/out schedule (*t* = −0.50), no better than a single 50-day EMA, and the permutation
  placebo p = **0.969**. The "conviction" width gate makes it strictly worse (*t* = −1.30).
  Every honest test points the same way: the ribbon carries no edge over the market's drift.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** There is no edge to trade. Even gross of costs the excess Sharpe
  (+0.315) trails buy-and-hold (+0.431); the long/short version is sharply negative. The
  lower drawdown is just the reduced exposure of being in cash ~28% of the time — a random
  schedule gets the same with a *worse* drawdown. Twelve moving averages dressed as a ribbon
  are a single trend filter with extra steps.
- **"Does the ribbon reveal conviction?" — BUSTED.** Guppy's signature claim — that a wide,
  parallel ribbon marks a high-conviction, continuing trend — is the part that performs
  *worst*: gating on ribbon width lowers Sharpe, CAGR and the *t*-stat. Width is not
  conviction; it is hindsight.
